content_list.content_text: All Quiet on the Western Front (1930)—a humanitarian drama about the First World War directed by Lewis Milestone (1895-1980) and based on the best-selling novel by Erich Maria Remarque—reflected the feelings of a generation of Americans who agreed with the lyrics of the song "I Didn't Raise My Boy to Be a Soldier." The film shows the conflict from the German point of view, and its villains are the politicians and civilians who use patriotism as an excuse to send young men to the front to die for nothing. The film also struck a deep chord with those who remembered the horrors of "the war to end all wars."

information.contentTitle: The final speech of The Great Dictator (1940)
information.contentText: Charles Chaplin (1889-1977) got the idea for The Great Dictator (1940) when his friend Alexander Korda noticed the physical resemblance between the Tramp and Adolf Hitler. Chaplin later discovered that he and Hitler had been born only a week apart, were the same height and weight, and had both been born into poverty and then risen to prominence. Chaplin decided to use this resemblance to attack Hitler when he learned of the policy of racial oppression the dictator was carrying out in Germany.

content_list.content_text: The star Lew Ayres (1908-1996) became so personally committed to pacifism that his career would later be damaged by the revelation that he remained opposed to World War II even when the country already thought otherwise. For much of the 1930s, despite—or because of—the news coming from Europe and Asia, films like The Man Who Reclaimed His Head (1934) portrayed world war as an evil promoted by dishonest politicians, corrupt arms dealers, and narrow-minded fanatics.

The rise of Nazism unsettled many people in Hollywood. Ironically, the studio heads, nearly all of them Jewish, had a personal style that might have made them more inclined to admire fascism—Harry Cohn of Columbia modeled his office on that of Benito Mussolini—were it not for the antisemitism that came with it. Producers such as Cohn, Walt Disney (a rare non-Jew in the industry), and Louis B. Mayer would have been far happier—as they were in the 1950s—fighting the communists, who seemed to them a more serious personal threat (through the spread of labor unions) than the fascists. Hollywood also wanted to ensure the commercial success of its films in Europe.

information.contentTitle: The patriotic broadcast in Foreign Correspondent (1940)
information.contentText: The rousing epilogue has the American hero, now devoted to the anti-fascist cause, broadcasting an urgent tribute to Britain's heroism under German air attack as sirens wail and bombs fall on London. "This is a big story," he says, "and you're part of it."

content_list.content_text: The intellectual and inflamed anti-Hollywood rhetoric of both the left and the right in the 1930s was also marked by antisemitism, so most of the studio heads preferred to keep quiet on political and religious matters. When Warner Bros. boldly produced The Life of Emile Zola (1937), which recounts the French writer's involvement in the Dreyfus affair, the fact that the defendant was Jewish is barely mentioned in the film.

content_list.title: Chaplin's inevitable parody
content_list.description:
It seemed inevitable that at some point Charlie Chaplin would play Hitler on screen; the two had been born only days apart and shared a certain distinctive feature on their faces. As critic and filmmaker Basil Wright put it: "Hitler's mistake of wearing the same mustache as Charlie left the director no choice: he had to seize that marvelous opportunity." The Great Dictator has not aged as well as other anti-Nazi films of the period, such as Pastor Hall (1940) and The Mortal Storm (1940), but the mere fact of its existence and the stills of Chaplin in costume hold a fascination that goes far beyond anything achieved by the film itself.

The film cost Chaplin 2 million dollars of his own money and two years of work, owing to threatening letters and pressure from the Hays Office and United Artists to drop the project. Its premiere, on October 15, 1940, was a major event, as it was the first talkie by one of the few film artists considered capable of standing up to Hitler at the time. The standout in the cast is Henry Daniell as the arrogant Garbitsch (a parody of Goebbels). Despite (or perhaps because of) his disagreements with Chaplin on set, his scenes carry an air of menace absent from the rest of the film, as when he declares: "You must stir up the people's anger. At this moment, violence against the Jews might make them stop thinking about their own stomachs." Chaplin later admitted: "Had I known of the actual horrors of the German concentration camps, I could not have made The Great Dictator; I could not have made fun of the homicidal insanity of the Nazis." Naturally, the film was banned in Germany, but Hitler himself watched it twice, alone. There is no record of his opinion of it.
content_list.credits: Original analysis adapted from the book Cinema: The Whole Story

content_list.content_text: Ironically, however, the popularity of All Quiet on the Western Front pushed Hollywood to make more films dealing with the situation in Germany at the time, in the hope of repeating the original's success. The Road Back (1937), Three Comrades (1938), and The Mortal Storm (1940) are unofficial sequels to All Quiet on the Western Front and show postwar Germany taking a violent political turn to the right.

quote.quote: ... Why should he put a musket to his shoulder, To kill another mother's darling boy...
quote.author: Excerpt from the song 'I Didn't Raise My Boy to Be a Soldier'

content_list.content_text: Warner Bros. was the most anti-Nazi studio of all, even closing its German branch—allegedly because antisemitic thugs had murdered its representative in the country. In 1939, the studio produced the incendiary Confessions of a Nazi Spy (1939), an exposé based on true events of German espionage in the United States that criticizes the Nazi leanings of the German American Bund, an American organization of sympathizers of German ultranationalism.

With another world war looking inevitable, the film industry responded by producing more films on the subject: Clarence Brown directed Idiot's Delight (1939), based on the play Idiot's Delight by Robert Sherwood (1896-1955), which tells the story of a group of Americans stranded in Europe when war breaks out, and it was already in theaters just a few months after the situation it portrays had taken place. What it implies is that the United States could not avoid getting involved in the conflict.

information.contentTitle: Promotional poster for Confessions of a Nazi Spy (1939)
information.contentText: As Hollywood's first anti-Nazi film, Confessions of a Nazi Spy (1939) was boldly released six months before war was declared in Europe.

content_list.content_text: American isolationists harshly criticized the way Hollywood seemed to lean toward the British side at the start of the war, especially when it came to English filmmakers such as Charlie Chaplin (1889-1977) with The Great Dictator (1940) and Alfred Hitchcock (1899-1980) with Foreign Correspondent (1940).

By 1941, Hollywood was perhaps better prepared to face a war than the American Army or any national defense agency. Resigned to the loss of the European market and aligned with President Roosevelt's "Good Neighbor" policy, the industry invested in all kinds of attempts to expand—such as the ill-fated, unfinished one.
content_list.content_credits: Summary based on the text by Kim Newman, published in the book "Cinema: The Whole Story" by Philip Kemp.

movies.title: The Great Dictator
movies.overview: Dictator Adenoid Hynkel tries to expand his empire while a poor Jewish barber tries to avoid persecution from Hynkel's regime.

movies.title: Foreign Correspondent
movies.overview: The European war was only beginning to erupt across national borders. Johnny Jones, an American crime reporter dispatched by his New York publisher to put a fresh spin on the drowsy dispatches emanating from overseas, has a nose for a good story—which promptly leads him to the crime of fascism and Nazi Germany's designs on European conquest. In attempting to learn more about a seemingly noble peace effort, Jones walks into the middle of an assassination, uncovers a spy ring and—not entirely coincidentally—falls in love.

movies.title: All Quiet on the Western Front
movies.original_title: All Quiet on the Western Front
movies.overview: A young soldier faces profound disillusionment in the soul-destroying horror of World War I. Together with several other young German soldiers, he experiences the horrors of war, such evil of which he had not conceived of when signing up to fight. They eventually become sad, tormented, and confused of their purpose.

movies.title: The Lady Vanishes
movies.overview: On a train headed for England a group of travelers is delayed by an avalanche. Holed up in a hotel in a fictional European country, young Iris befriends elderly Miss Froy. When the train resumes, Iris suffers a bout of unconsciousness and wakes to find the old woman has disappeared. The other passengers ominously deny Miss Froy ever existed, so Iris begins to investigate with another traveler and, as the pair sleuth, romantic sparks fly.

movies.original_title: The Man Who Reclaimed His Head
movies.title: The Man Who Reclaimed His Head
movies.overview: A writer discovers he's being used as a pawn by greedy businessmen. Director Edward Ludwig's 1934 drama stars Claude Rains, Lionel Atwill, Joan Bennett, Henry O'Neill and Wallace Ford.
